Qg2# delivers it directly: the queen checks from g2, and the king can't step to f1 (your rook), h1 (his own rook), or h2 (your queen). drills.coachNote: Black's queen on c5 still has that clean diagonal to c2, where it checks your king and your rook on d1 has nobody else guarding it. You played f3, a pawn move that does nothing about that, and after Qc2+ you're pushed to Kh3 and then Qxd1 just takes the rook for free. Rd4 was the better idea: it lifts the rook off the back rank and out of the queen's reach while getting active, planning Ke6, Rf4, and meeting Black's queenside expansion with your own king marching up via Kg3. Whenever a piece is only defended by your king, moving a pawn doesn't fix that — move the piece.
drills.threat: Black's queen on c5 still has a clear path to c2 with check, and your rook on d1 is unguarded but for the king.

drills.explanation: Re2 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Kf3 ran into Bd5+, costing about 17.3 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs koleapapa (479) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Before you even moved, Black's queen on d2 had a clean fork — it hits your rook on e3 on the diagonal and your bishop on d3 on the file, so one of them falls to a passive move. Kf3 ignores the fork completely and also steps onto the d5-f3 diagonal, so Black answers Bd5+, then Be4 and Bxe4+ tears through, turning your comfortable +4.5 into near-disaster. Re2 meets the fork head-on by offering the queen trade: after Qxe2+ Bxe2 Kg7 Nxf7 Kxf7 you're simply up material in a clean, winning endgame. When one piece attacks two of yours, answer the fork directly instead of a king move that solves nothing.
drills.threat: Black's queen on d2 is forking your rook on e3 and your bishop on d3 at once.

drills.explanation: Qf7 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Qxc5 ran into f4+, costing about 12.9 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs koleapapa (479) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: You had Black completely boxed in — king stuck on h8, rook on e8 unable to do anything useful — and the winning plan was to keep tightening that net rather than stop for material. Qxc5 grabs a pawn but eases the pressure, letting Black generate a disruptive check and kick your queen around with ...b6, which is why the evaluation drops by nearly 13 pawns even though you're still better. Qf7 keeps the squeeze on: it forces Rb8, brings your knight to d7, and the attack just keeps rolling instead of giving Black a breather. When you have the enemy king trapped like this, finish the job before you go pawn-hunting.
drills.threat: Black's king is stuck on h8 with no escape squares, and the rook on e8 is tied down.

drills.explanation: Bd7 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Nh6 left that piece hanging: after Qxh6 it's simply lost.
drills.title: vs magdyis (520) — Grob Opening
drills.coachNote: The c1-h6 diagonal was wide open — nothing on d2, e3, f4, or g5 — so any piece you dropped onto h6 was simply going to be captured for free. You played Nh6 straight into that, and Qxh6 just wins the knight outright, costing you roughly 5 pawns of evaluation for nothing. The engine wanted Bd7 instead: quiet development that stays off that diagonal entirely and keeps the position balanced while you prep ...c5. Before placing a piece on a square, always glance down the open lines pointed at it, especially ones a major piece already occupies.
drills.threat: White's queen on c1 sits on a completely open diagonal running all the way to h6.

drills.explanation: Qh4+ forks the king on e1 and the king on e1 — one of them falls next move. In the game, Rd2 ran into Nxe3, costing about 5.0 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs magdyis (520) — Grob Opening
drills.coachNote: White was hoping to hide behind that knight on d1, using it to shore up e3 and f2 while the king sat passively on e1. Rd2 lets White play Nxe3, attacking your rook and forcing a trade-down sequence (Rxg2 Nxg2) that cashes in some material but drops nearly 5 pawns of your advantage compared to finishing the attack outright. Qh4+ was the real punch: it forces Nf2, and then exf2+ Kf1 Rd1+ Ke2 rips the king out into the open while you keep gaining material with every move. With the enemy king this exposed, look for the check that drags it out before you start trading pieces off.
drills.threat: White's king on e1 is boxed in behind an undeveloped knight on d1, and your pawn on e3 is one tempo from breaking through.

drills.explanation: Re5 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, d3 ran into Kxe3, costing about 7.8 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs Dishantt7 (605) — Caro Kann Defense
drills.coachNote: Your rook on e3 was only safe because your pawn on d4 guarded that square — the moment that pawn moves, White's king just walks in and takes the rook for free. That's exactly what d3 does: it pushes the defender away, so Kxe3 wins your rook outright and flips a comfortable +2.6 into real trouble, a swing of nearly 8 pawns. Re5 was the move — it repositions the rook to an active square without touching the d4 pawn, and after Bc2 Rb5 b3 Rc8 Be4 you keep both the extra pawn and rook activity. Before you push a pawn, check whether it's the only thing stopping an enemy piece from grabbing something nearby.
drills.threat: White's king on f2 is one step from your rook on e3, held back only by your pawn on d4.

drills.explanation: dxe4 simply wins the pawn on e4 — it wasn't adequately defended. In the game, Nf6 ran into e5, costing about 5.1 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs Dishantt7 (605) — Caro Kann Defense
drills.coachNote: Your d5 pawn is already attacking White's pawn on e4, but if you don't take it, White gets to push e5 next — forking your bishop on d6 and the knight you just developed to f6. That's exactly what happens after Nf6: e5 hits both pieces, you save the bishop with Bc7, and exf6 gxf6 leaves your kingside pawns damaged and your structure worse, a 5-pawn swing for nothing. dxe4 simply grabs the pawn while it's free, and after Ne1 Nf6 d3 exd3 Nxd3 you're comfortably fine with an extra pawn in hand. When a central pawn is hanging, take it before the opponent gets to use it as a forking weapon instead.
drills.threat: White's pawn on e4 can push to e5 next, forking your bishop on d6 and anything you put on f6.
